results.summary: This Verilog design implements free-running oscillators using combinational loops with frequency dividers to bring outputs below 50 kHz. It also includes a true random number generator (TRNG) based on jitter from the oscillators. To test, select an oscillator via input pins and measure frequency on output pins; the TRNG output can be observed for random bit generation. The project is intended to verify simulation results against real silicon behaviour.

This Verilog design generates a PWM signal with duty cycle configurable in 12.5% steps based on a 3-bit input. It requires an external 10 MHz clock and can be tested by applying input combinations and observing the output on an oscilloscope. The design uses incremental duty cycles from 12.5% to 100% depending on the input code. It is intended for educational purposes and general PWM generation applications.

This Wokwi project uses an OR gate to drive a seven-segment display to spell the letter J. It requires eight switches for input and a seven-segment display as external hardware. Testing involves flipping switches to produce the desired segment pattern. The design is a minimal educational example of combinational logic driving an output display.

This Verilog design implements Wolfram's Rule 30 cellular automaton in hardware and displays the evolving pattern on a VGA monitor. It uses a 320-bit register updated in parallel each row, starting from a single seed at the top centre. Four colour palettes are selectable via input pins. The design requires a VGA PMOD and a 25 MHz clock, and it creates a chaotic triangular pattern that expands downward.

This project implements an analog buffer using two inverters (one large and one small) from Matt's analog course. It has a single analog input and output, requiring no external hardware beyond a power supply. Testing involves applying an analog voltage to the input and observing the output. It is a simple transistor-level design intended for educational use and characterization on silicon.

This Wokwi-based puzzle game uses seven switches to control a seven-segment display, where each switch toggles a segment and its neighbours. The goal is to make the display show all digits 0 through 9. It requires seven microswitches and a seven-segment LED display as external hardware. The design is an interactive educational demonstration of combinatorial and sequential logic.

This Verilog design generates a controllable Archimedean spiral pattern on a VGA monitor. It requires a 25 MHz clock and a VGA PMOD for output. The input pins adjust the foreground/background colours and the rotation speed. It is a demonstration of hardware-generated geometric animation.

This Verilog design classifies images of digits 0–7 using the 16 most significant pixels of an 8×8 image. The classification result is displayed on a seven-segment display. It requires no external hardware beyond the Tiny Tapeout board and can be tested by setting the feature inputs to predefined patterns. The design is a simple example of hardware-based pattern recognition.

This Verilog design implements a 4-neuron spiking neural network (SNN) accelerator using the leaky integrate-and-fire model with off-chip weights. It requires an RP2040 microcontroller to stream weights and perform Hebbian learning updates. The design operates at 50 MHz and processes a full network pass in 28 cycles. It outputs spikes on eight output pins and includes control signals for synchronization with the RP2040.

This Verilog design implements a counter that counts up to 10 at one-second intervals, displaying the result on a seven-segment display. It also includes input compare pins for skew measurement and requires programmable delay lines on inputs. However, the project documentation is incomplete, so the exact behavior cannot be confirmed. It is intended as a test chip for characterization.
